evidence.fact: Off-the-shelf OKR agents already generate structured objectives and key results aligned to a stated vision, for teams or businesses. This covers the drafting sub-step end to end.
Agent workflows can analyze past goals and key business metrics and then recommend realistic objectives and key results. The manager still has to choose priorities and accept the result.

Mainstream goal-management platforms such as Asana and Lattice link goals to projects and performance reviews, so drafted goals and deadlines can go straight into existing systems. Vendor AI features were not checked against official documentation.

Commercial AI takeoff tools (ConstructConnect Takeoff Boost, Togal.AI, Trimble, Handoff H1 in July 2026) read blueprints and produce quantity and material takeoffs automatically. Most of the speed and accuracy figures come from the vendors, and estimators' work is moving toward reviewing the AI's output.
Handoff says its H1 model does autonomous blueprint takeoffs and matches experienced estimators on residential plans. This claim comes from a press release and has not been independently checked.

Cost estimating is generally not a licensed occupation in Canada, though certification is often expected. Registration is required only in a few places, such as for quantity surveyors in Victoria, Australia. I did not check US or UK rules in this search.

O*NET lists this as a core sonographer duty: preparing the patient, explaining the procedure, moving the patient onto the table, cleaning the skin, applying gel and positioning the patient. Nearly all of these steps are hands-on work done with the patient in the room.

Commercial conversational AI (for example, Patient Prism) can give radiology exam preparation instructions and answer patients' questions before the exam. That covers only the explaining part of the task. The vendor's claims have not been independently evaluated.

Studies of AI-generated information about abdominal ultrasound find that it is fast, but its accuracy and reliability are still uncertain. A commentary recommends using chatbots only to supplement human patient education.
Retorio sells retail-focused AI roleplay in which virtual customers push back, object and surprise trainees during objection-handling and upselling practice. This is vendor marketing.

Born Digital's AI roleplay tools for store and call-center staff score tone, accuracy, empathy, policy compliance and how the situation was resolved, so an agent could run the practice and feedback steps on its own. This is vendor marketing.

RetailDoc's SalesRX offers AI roleplay training for retail associates. Its customer case study reports that 99% of associates said they improved, which is a self-reported vendor figure. The supervisor still has to watch live sales on the floor and coach in person.

Rental technician job postings describe the work as hands-on: setting bindings to the boot and to safety standards (sometimes with certification), fitting boots with a foot sizer, and checking gear for damage before and after rental.
Texada (vendor-reported, launched March 2026) offers AI damage detection that compares check-out and check-in photos. A person still has to take the photos and do any repair or adjustment.
Record360's 360AI is human-in-the-loop: the AI flags possible damage and people make the final call, so it only assists with the inspection step.

Commercial AI agents pull data from invoices, check it, match it to purchase orders and send it for approval. Vendors claim they can read messy handwriting, but I found no independent test of handwriting accuracy. They report 95%+ accuracy overall and say line items are harder to read than header fields.

Payroll AI agents (Deloitte's listing on AWS Marketplace) check timesheets, worker classification and tax withholding, and flag errors before payroll runs. This covers the 'work with pay records' sub-step.
Invoice-processing agents check that data matches existing records and send a person a review request when something looks wrong. A human still reviews the exceptions.

Atlassian's Jira Service Management ships Rovo agents. A Service Triage agent sets urgency and priority and recommends request types. An Ops Guide agent helps limit incident impact and runs post-incident reviews. This covers the workflow analysis and prioritization sub-steps (vendor claim).

A consultancy built a custom Rovo agent that prioritizes backlog work items in place of manual review. This shows that setting priorities can be partly delegated end to end, but a manager still accepts the result and enforces it with staff (consultancy case study; results not shown).

Rovo agents are positioned to automate triage and routine requests so IT teams can do higher-value work. Directing staff, setting deadlines people will meet, and enforcing standards still need human managerial authority and trust (vendor event listing).

Microsoft Planner's Project Manager agent, in preview, drafts status report emails and summaries of progress, milestones, blockers and next steps from plan data. People can then co-edit the reports in Loop and share them.
Atlassian shows how to build a Rovo agent that pulls Jira and Confluence data to write project health, milestone and risk summaries for PMOs and executives.

These products produce draft reports for people to review and edit before sharing. A manager still has to check accuracy, interpret context and approve the result, which is the review half of this task.

The rules for registered apprenticeship programs (29 CFR 29.5) are a published checklist: a written plan, work-process schedules, related-instruction outlines, equal-opportunity compliance under 29 CFR part 30 and a complaint contact. An agent can map program documents against these items.

State sample standards tie each program provision to a specific 29.5(b) subsection, so checking documents for compliance can largely be automated. Judging how a program actually runs, such as on-the-job supervision and apprentice interviews, still needs a human.

Commercial compliance agents already track mandatory training completion and certification expirations and run gap analyses across HR, policy and training records. This is a vendor's claim, not an independent test. I found no dedicated AI product for apprenticeship compliance review.

Paradox's hospitality platform and its Olivia assistant already handle high-volume hotel hiring from front desk to housekeeping. Olivia screens applicants with knockout questions, schedules interviews against recruiter calendars, sends reminders, and produces offer letters and onboarding documents.
Third-party reviews say Olivia also coordinates video interviews and hiring events, so an agent can run most of the pipeline end to end. A human still usually decides who gets hired.

NYC Local Law 144 requires a bias audit, a published audit summary, and notice to candidates, who can ask for an alternative selection process. This, together with employer liability for hiring decisions, keeps a human accountable for the final choice. The EU AI Act also classes hiring AI as high-risk with human oversight duties, but my searches did not confirm this.

Commercial AI tools such as Mentalyc and TherapyFuel already draft the written plan from session notes or chart diagnoses. They write the goals, objectives and interventions and track progress on each goal. Vendors say the output is a draft that the clinician must review using their own clinical judgment.

Illinois' Wellness and Oversight for Psychological Resources Act (2025) bars AI from making therapeutic decisions on its own. It also bars AI from producing treatment plans or recommendations unless a licensed professional reviews and approves them, with fines of up to $10,000 per violation.

Comparisons of AI tools for therapists in 2026 describe them as documentation and drafting aids that leave the clinical reasoning to the therapist. Carrying out the plan means delivering therapy, which depends on direct contact with clients and the trust built there.

In December 2025 OCLC added AI suggestions for DDC and LCC classification numbers and LCSH subject headings to Record Manager and Connexion. Catalogers accept or ignore each suggestion and verify it. Pilot libraries reported saving up to 20 minutes per title (OCLC's own figure).

When tested on LCSH, Sears, LCC, DDC and Cutter assignment, ChatGPT and Copilot gave headings that were not specific enough, used unauthorized terms, and built malformed synthetic headings. The authors recommend using them as aids, with human review.

A DCMI 2026 paper reports that LLMs produce LCSH strings that look plausible but break policy. It proposes connecting Claude through MCP to Library of Congress linked-data APIs to check authority headings, so agent pipelines that validate their own output are possible but a human still checks the result.

Elicit, Consensus, Scite and Scopus AI already search the scholarly literature, build literature matrices and write summarized literature reviews with real citations. This covers the main sub-steps of compiling bibliographies and preparing abstracts.

These tools rely mainly on abstracts and open-access full text, and their vendors warn that they can hallucinate or produce inaccurate summaries. A human still has to check the citations and the abstracts before they are used.

Current tools cover large indexes of papers (over 138 million for Elicit and over 250 million for Consensus) and offer deep literature review features. The task is fully digital and needs no physical presence or licensed sign-off.

Commercial agentic RCM products say they check eligibility, assemble prior-authorization packets, fix denials and track appeals. They also say humans stay in the loop for key decisions and that unclear cases are escalated for manual review. These are vendor claims and have not been independently verified.

Pharmacy billing technicians spend much of their time on payer rejections, eligibility checks and prior authorizations, including talking with insurance companies. All of this is digital or done by phone.

Technician billing work is covered by state board of pharmacy rules and employer policy. The material found did not show a rule requiring a licensed person to sign claim submissions. Pharmacist verification applies to dispensing, not to billing.

Under nursing or medical direction, psychiatric aides give hands-on routine care. This includes help with bathing, dressing, grooming, feeding and toileting, physical checks, and restraining patients to prevent injury.
A California DDS duty statement for this type of role lists helping individuals with feeding, toileting, grooming and appearance. All of these require physical presence.

Pennsylvania's Office of Developmental Programs warns that AI companion bots pose privacy, emotional and safety risks for people with intellectual disabilities. This means software can only play a limited supporting role, such as caregiver chatbots or activity prompts.

In O*NET-based job descriptions, psychiatric aides walk with patients to and from exams and treatments, keep them in assigned areas, and may restrain violent patients. This is physical, in-person supervision that an agent without a body cannot do.
Aides watch patients for unusual or harmful behaviour and physically restrain or help them to prevent injury. Escorting depends on being there in person and building trust with the patient.

Aides work under nursing and medical staff. No specific licence requires a human to sign off on escorting, but the task cannot be done without physical presence. Software can only help at the edges, such as scheduling or transport logistics.

Qualcomm's NRF 2025 demo shows a smart pharmacy kiosk that helps shoppers find items, book flu shots and get health information. This means an agent can do the product lookup and give directions without a person.

CJ Olive Young (July 2026) has an AI avatar kiosk that checks stock, finds products in the store and recommends items in eight languages. Shoppers can serve themselves, but the kiosk does not walk them to the shelf or greet them in person.

Intel lists an AI chatbot kiosk for pharmacy stores, so locating products with conversational AI is a real product category. The physical parts, greeting someone on the floor and walking them to the shelf, still need a human.
Automating food plating and delivery to tables needs dedicated robotic hardware, such as SoftBank's STEAMA/FLAMA cooking robots or delivery robots. A software-only AI agent can't do this.
Getting a plated dish to a customer's table takes physical robotic systems like overhead rails or mobile robots with arms. Even these robots are still described as limited spot solutions.
A patent on robotic service systems describes placing dishes directly at a customer's table as a physical problem that robotics still needs to solve.

O*NET lists 'Carry food supplies, equipment, and utensils to and from storage and work areas' as a core task for Food Preparation Workers (35-2021.00), with importance 87. The task is about physically moving items around a kitchen.

The occupation does hands-on, non-cooking food prep and stocking work in a physical kitchen. A software-only agent with no robotic body cannot move supplies, so its only possible contribution is a minor side job like inventory lists.
AI ordering systems combine voice recognition, a large language model and QR codes so customers can order without an app. They can take drink orders end to end through a kiosk or a phone.

Robotic and kiosk bars take orders by tablet, touchscreen or voice commands. A UK commentary says these systems are not a full replacement for human bartenders, and some chains say they will not adopt them.

State rules require bar staff to refuse alcohol to anyone under 21 or apparently intoxicated, which means checking ID and judging intoxication in person. Bars also face dram shop liability for serving such patrons.
Generative AI menu tools suggest dishes, flavor pairings, prices and menu descriptions from consumer-demand data and simple inputs, so an agent can produce the material staff would discuss.

Some AI menu tools connect to POS systems to pull sales and inventory data, but Toast advises operators to check AI-generated menus for practicality and cost before using them, so a human still reviews the result.

AI menu planning is sold as support for the people deciding the menu (data analysis and suggestions), not as a replacement for the staff discussion. The conversation itself and the host's first-hand guest feedback stay with humans.
The assistance porters give to passengers with reduced mobility is hands-on and in person: staff meet them at call points, help with check-in, and walk them all the way to their seat on the aircraft.
Autonomous wheelchairs are only at an early stage. Rome Fiumicino's four are run by assistance staff, and Dubai's is still being tested. Both are robotics, which the reference AI agents do not have.

The digital help now available comes from apps such as Be My Eyes and Aira, which use AI and remote agents for information and navigation. That only adds to in-person escort and baggage handling; it does not replace them.

Ohai.ai's AI connects to Google, Outlook and Apple calendars. It finds free time, schedules events, avoids overlaps and pulls dates and deadlines out of forwarded emails. A third-party reviewer says it also helps coordinate drop-off and pickup, with reminders.

Skylight syncs several family calendars, and its paid Sidekick AI turns forwarded school emails and paper handouts into events. A reviewer notes that such tools do not answer the coach or set up the carpool, so human coordination is still needed.
Ohai.ai is described as an AI household assistant for family scheduling and household logistics.
Recyclers, which are cash-handling machines rather than software agents, can prepare tills at the start of a shift. Someone still has to handle the physical drawer and the cash.

In patented cash-handling devices, a cashier or manager physically puts the drawer into the machine. The device then counts the cash and checks it against the expected amount, so the counting is done by hardware.

Brink's recyclers automate till dispensing and counting at shift start and close. A software-only AI agent can at most read the device's reports or the POS expected-float figures to help reconcile, and cannot count physical cash itself.
Vendor says its storefront AI assistant learns a store's products, policies and FAQs, and handles shipping, order-tracking and return questions on its own.

Microsoft's Store Operations Agent helps store staff find answers on store procedures, order status and inventory. This supports in-store question answering, but a human still deals with the customer face to face.
Retail AI phone assistants answer questions about store hours, orders and return policies, and pass complex cases to staff. Edge cases still need a human.

Cassidy's vendor page describes a payroll reconciliation agent. Before funds go out, it compares current payroll against prior periods at the employee and aggregate levels. It also matches outbound payroll debits against bank statements and journal postings.

Spendflo's bank reconciliation agent pairs payment and ledger records, flags unmatched items with likely causes, and produces a period summary for sign-off. Accountants still accept the matches and make adjusting entries, and controllers sign off.
Oracle Fusion Cash Management reconciles payroll bank accounts automatically using matching and tolerance rules. Exceptions still need human resolution.
Order-intake agents built on Dynamics 365 use MCP to match customers, items and quantities against ERP records. Items they cannot match go to a review screen where a person corrects them.
Workist's Order Agent processes more than half of Primavera's orders fully automatically. When order data conflicts with master data, a salesperson reviews the order before it goes to the ERP.
A multi-agent system with a customer-validation agent uses business rules and fuzzy matching to find the right ERP customer IDs. The vendor reports that 85% of order workflows are fully automated.

Vendor buyer's guides from 2026 describe AI recruiting agents that run hiring workflows from a goal, including screening applications against criteria and changing the criteria when too few candidates match, with little human input. These are vendor claims and have not been independently checked.

NYC Local Law 144 covers tools that substantially assist or replace discretionary hiring decisions. Employers must get an independent bias audit within the past year, publish a summary of it and notify candidates. It does not ban automated screening, and the sources found do not show it requires human review.

Commentary from 2026 says the EU AI Act and NYC LL144 put compliance duties on hiring AI. I did not confirm from a primary source that the EU AI Act classes recruitment AI as high-risk with human-oversight duties, so this rests on background knowledge. That is why barrier_accountability is set to true and the work is rated partial rather than full delegation.

Superunit says its agent 'Ava' runs employment verification end to end by phone, email and fax. The company reports 200k verifications across 17 countries, about 70% completed, most within a day. These are the vendor's own figures.
Bright Horizons uses Phenom's AI voice screening agent to run reference checks at scale. Concerning responses are flagged for a recruiter to review, so a human still checks the output.

Under the FCRA, the applicant must receive a written disclosure and give authorization before a consumer report is obtained. The law does not require a human staff member to make the request, and these rules generally don't apply when the employer calls references itself.

Salesforce says Agentforce for Field Service lets customers schedule, reschedule or cancel service appointments around the clock in natural language, with the booking finalized without human involvement. This is a vendor claim, not an independent evaluation.
Fieldcode presents AI voice agents that take field-service requests, check them and pass them directly into scheduling workflows. This is also vendor material.

Fieldproxy's marketing says its AI voice agents answer inbound calls, qualify requests and book jobs, and that it assigns work by technician skills, availability and location. These claims are not independently verified, and no source covering trucking or freight dispatch turned up.

Pactum's AI agents negotiate with hundreds of suppliers at once over chat, following policies set by humans. This is vendor marketing, and it covers routine commercial terms, not technical discussions about products.
NEC's automated negotiation AI is a Gartner-cited use case. It automates adjusting delivery schedules with suppliers, a narrow, rule-bound sub-step.

Procurement sources say AI agents work well for transactional negotiations with clear parameters, but strategic supplier discussions still need human judgment and relationship skills. No source showed agents running vendor product meetings, which often include in-person demos and handling samples.

The vendors that automate weld-path generation (Path Robotics, TetraGen, ABAGY, CENIT FastSuite) all rely on robot cells with 3D vision. A software agent without a body cannot hold a torch or join metal; at most it can look up procedures or settings, which is a small share of the time.
Even the AI-driven robotic welding systems listed in 2026 are described as not yet fully autonomous, and they need dedicated robot hardware. They do not fit varied general repair work done on site.

OSHA 1910.252 requires on-site safety work for hot work: moving combustibles within 35 ft, having extinguishers ready, and posting fire watchers for at least 30 minutes afterward. All of this needs physical presence. It covers hot-work safety; the searches found no welder licence requirement for general maintenance.

Camera-based AI occupancy software can find occupied and free bays, including in unmarked areas, using standard IP cameras. That covers only the monitoring side of space use, not the cleaning or tidying itself.

Parking AI platforms offer live dashboards showing available, occupied and reserved spaces by zone, plus APIs that feed signage. An agent could watch these and flag problems, but a person still has to sweep, remove debris and move cones or vehicles on site.
Bosch AI cameras can monitor parking bays without sensors fitted to each bay, which helps with space-use analytics. They do no physical cleaning or rearranging.

Measuring, weighing and counting on packing lines is automated by dedicated machines, not software agents. Examples are combined checkweigher and vision systems (±0.5 g at 150 packs/min) and line-scan counters. A hand packer still has to put items on scales and count them by hand. A software-only agent can only help with record-keeping, tally arithmetic and checking tolerances.
Vision counting machines can count products into boxes at high speed (vendor claims up to 100,000 per hour at more than 99% accuracy). This is robotics and machinery, not the reference agent.

NIST Handbook 133 sets the rules for testing net contents of packaged goods. It mainly governs compliance testing by officials and does not require a licensed human to weigh or count during routine packing.
Saleo launched an AI Demo Agent in January 2026. Saleo describes it as a fully conversational agent that runs product demos on its own, in several languages, 24/7, with live co-browsing for buyers.

In 2026 there are several AI demo agent tools that build demos or present them to buyers, including Consensus, Storylane, Navattic, Naoma and Saleo. Setup takes days to weeks and needs a human to configure and approve the content.
Sales reps worry that AI demo agents will botch demos or pass along cold leads. This suggests that live, high-stakes demos to field staff and key customers still need human delivery and review.

A paid funeral usher job posting lists in-person duties: greeting families and guests, directing them to the service area and restrooms, handing out memorial folders, moving flowers and setting up extra chairs. All of these require physical presence.
Funeral directors discreetly guide immediate family to the front rows. This seating is done in person, with tact, for grieving people.

Ushers are often the first point of contact. They help guests find their designated seats and get around the venue, which is face-to-face hospitality that a software-only agent cannot do. An agent could at most draft a seating chart or digital signage.

ServiceNow says its AI agent resolves 90% of inbound IT tickets at its own employee help desk. It handles password resets, account unlocks, software access requests and connectivity issues end to end. This figure is reported by the vendor and has not been independently audited.
Ivanti's April 2026 release put an agentic AI service-desk agent into commercial use for autonomous ticket resolution.

A 2026 industry roundup says the best platforms resolve 40% or more of incoming tickets without a human. Routine Level 1 requests get automated first, and humans still handle escalations and complex or hardware-related malfunctions.

Under NRC rule 10 CFR 35.25, a licensee that lets supervised people use radioactive (byproduct) material must teach them radiation safety and periodically review their work. Supervision must come from an authorized user or licensee, so a human remains responsible.

In accredited imaging programs, a qualified technologist must directly supervise students until they reach competency. That technologist reviews the procedure, checks the patient's condition, is physically present and approves the procedure or images. This is the general imaging-education pattern (JRCERT); I did not find the nuclear-medicine-specific JRCNMT text.

Hospital clinical-education policies require certified technologists to supervise student patient care, and to be present for some procedures regardless of the student's competency. An AI agent can only help with teaching materials, quizzes, scheduling and record-keeping.

Exercise-prescription platforms like Physitrack, MedBridge and Wibbi use AI to speed up building and personalizing rehab programs. Clinicians still choose and approve each exercise and stay responsible for treatment planning and red-flag screening.

Alaska's statute lets athletic trainers practice only under a licensed physician's direction, given through verbal or written orders, treatment plans, protocols or standing orders. Trainers must refer athletes to another licensed professional when athletic training is contraindicated.

Illinois bills describe athletic trainers providing rehabilitation on the direction or prescription of a physician, or in collaboration with one. Putting a program into practice means hands-on physical medicine and rehabilitation techniques with the athlete in person.

Job postings for sterile processing and medical equipment preparers describe hands-on work: handling instruments, assembling trays, and moving supplies to hospital units and the operating room. Moving patients and setting up traction are physical bedside duties of the same kind. An AI agent with no body can do none of this. At most it could handle a small piece of transport-request logistics.
The role sends clean and sterile supplies to inpatient units and collects contaminated items. That means being on the floor in person, alongside patients and staff.

The payout math is easy to automate. Payout calculators and casino management systems that reconcile expected table results with chip-bank changes already exist. But at a live table the dealer must first see the physical chips bet on the layout, and then pay out in physical chips, which an agent without a body cannot do.
Patents for winning-bet payout calculators show that live-table payouts are computed by the dealer from bets on the physical table. The tools only assist with that calculation.
Card game dealers must hold a licence. For example, Montana requires an annual dealer licence from the state Department of Justice. Casino payouts are handled only by licensed staff.

FoundFastApp can turn one photo of several items into separate records with description, brand and category. It also matches found items to lost-item reports and alerts owners by SMS or email. The digital record-keeping and owner-contact steps can be automated, but a person still has to collect, photograph and store each item.
Traista offers AI matching on description, date and location, with image recognition and automatic categorization. Staff still have to log found items and upload photos themselves.
AI image-matching systems are used for lost luggage at airports. Physical handling and returning items to owners remain human jobs.

LLM-based museum guides and chatbots already answer visitor questions, recommend routes and support wayfinding in many languages on kiosks and phones. Physically leading visitors still needs a robot or a person.
An LLM-based guide system maps visitor requests to answers or to location and navigation codes. Research prototypes that physically lead visitors around museums rely on robots.
Cities that license tour guides attach the licence to giving guided tours. Simply giving directions or information to visitors does not require a human by law.

Commercial AI voice agents (e.g., Aloware) qualify prospects, run campaign- or CRM-triggered outbound calls, and book appointments directly into Google Calendar, Cal.com or Calendly using real-time availability, so the whole scheduling task can run end to end.

Documented builds on Vapi/n8n show an agent calling a lead list, explaining services, booking meetings on a sales lead's calendar and sending confirmations with meeting links, all without a human in the loop.

The FCC's February 2024 Declaratory Ruling puts AI-generated voices under TCPA 'artificial or prerecorded voice' rules. Marketing calls need prior express (written) consent, so cold outreach without consent in practice still needs a human caller. The task itself requires no physical presence.
Vendors say their AI answering-service agents answer every call, record messages and send urgent inquiries to the right person. These are marketing claims, not independent tests.

Vendors say AI voice agents route calls based on what the caller says, transfer or escalate urgent issues, and take detailed messages for follow-up. They also say emergencies, complaints and sensitive calls still need a human.
A guide says caller details are transcribed and sent to email, CRM or help desk automatically, and warns the AI only works as well as the business information it is given.

O*NET lists this as a core helper task. Related duties are cutting and threading pipe, setting pipe in hangers, drilling openings in walls and floors, and supplying or holding materials and tools. All of these are hands-on work.
A plumber-helper job posting says the work is about 70% standing and 25% walking. It also requires climbing, kneeling, crouching, crawling, reaching and handling, so it needs a person on site.

Rule-based software already generates piping isometrics, dimensions and bills of materials from 3D models. That covers design-office layout work, not the helper's physical help with layout, assembly and installation in the field.

Ross mixers can come with a PLC control panel and a touchscreen HMI/SCADA package that handle recipe selection, mixing, heating and vacuum control, and log data. Some adjustments can therefore be made through software, but an operator still works the touchscreen and controls on site.

In a retrofit, a manually run food mixer was given an HMI+PLC that stores up to 99 recipes and has manual and automatic modes. It still pauses for manual ingredient additions, which shows the equipment is run by hand on the plant floor.

Food-processing automation runs on plant PLCs and local control systems. These are operational networks that a general-purpose AI agent normally cannot reach, so pressing switches and turning knobs remains a physical, on-site task.

Bühler's Finer S Edition 26 five-roll refiner uses digital sensors to watch the process in real time and adjusts roll speed, pressure and temperature on its own. So the machine's built-in controls already handle the parameter tuning, not an outside AI agent.

HDM/MacIntyre refiner/conches save process recipes in plant PLC software that runs on Siemens or Allen-Bradley interfaces. These are plant-floor control systems that a software agent would not normally be able to reach. The operator still has to load the batches, take samples and run the machine on site.

Commercial refiner/conche units of 500 to 2000 kg are run from a touchscreen PLC, and the target particle size changes with the type of product. The work is physical machine operation on the production floor, and no licence or sign-off rule requires a particular person to do it.

Existing AI CPR tools, such as purpose-built chatbots and apps like CPR AI, only coach a human through compressions and AED use with voice or visual prompts and feedback. The person still does the physical rescue.
Most US states require lifeguards to hold Red Cross or equivalent lifeguard, CPR and first-aid certification. Massachusetts requires annual CPR/BLS for Professional Rescuers certification.
AI CPR-guidance apps can improve bystander performance, but someone physically present still has to act, and calling emergency services stays essential.

Vision AI products such as Tiliter Cleensight and FieldProxy score cleanliness from photos taken by staff or from fixed cameras. A person or installed hardware still has to capture the scene, so an AI agent can help with the inspection but cannot carry it out alone.

Oregon's daily aquatic facility checklist is an on-site walk-through before opening. It checks that decks and walkways are clean and free of debris and that drains and skimmers are clear. This needs someone physically present.

Health-department self-inspection checklists require decks to be free of algae, biofilm and dirt. Facility staff do these checks by sight and touch, and no license is required for a human to sign the routine cleanliness check.

Dough is automated with dedicated robots and machines (Pazzi's robotic pizzerias, Zume's Doughbot press), not with software-only AI agents. The task needs physical mixing, kneading, dividing and shaping.
Industrial dough lines use a vacuum filler and a tray-loading robot to divide and handle dough balls, which shows the core work is physical handling.
Zume Pizza used an automated dough press to make crusts faster. This is physical automation, not an AI agent working through software.
Usher job postings describe this task as physically placing event and venue signage, putting up or taking down posters, and setting up and staffing information tables or kiosks in the lobby.
Washington State's usher job specification lists staffing kiosks or stations and doing set-up and tear-down, all on-site duties.

Venue digital-signage software such as CultureSuite pulls event data and updates screens automatically when events change. This covers only the digital-display part of the task, which is a small share of what ushers do here.

Published rubrics already define how K-12 tools and programs are judged for teaching fit and for federal privacy law (FERPA, COPPA). An agent can apply them and draft the analysis and reports, but administrators still have to do the review.
Vendor guides for evaluating programs call for structured pilots and real-world checks in schools, which humans have to carry out and interpret, before a district adopts a program.

State law (for example Ohio and Michigan) and district contracts require in-person formal classroom observations and walkthroughs by administrators. Judging teaching methods therefore needs someone physically in the classroom.

A 2025 study of AI grading on a handwritten general chemistry exam found high agreement between AI and human graders on text and reaction questions. Agreement was lower on numerical and graphical items, so the authors recommend human review of partially correct or ambiguous answers.
Gradescope's AI groups similar handwritten answers, including chemistry diagrams, so they can be marked in batches. It gave no help with grading paragraph-type answers.

University of Utah policy says AI may not be the sole or final grading authority. The instructor of record has to review AI-assisted output before grades are finalized, and student work counts as a FERPA-protected record.

OpenAI Academy runs sessions on building workspace agents for higher-ed faculty and researchers. These agents help with prep work such as drafting, research synthesis and admin, not with the faculty collaboration itself.

Agents in higher education are said to speed up research workflows: literature work, simulated research teams like Stanford's Virtual Lab, and lower per-paper costs at Johns Hopkins' Agent Laboratory. These are vendor-reported claims, but they suggest AI can help with research tasks while colleagues still make the decisions.
Faculty teaching collaboratives are still run as human peer-learning communities. AI shows up as the topic and as a shared resource, not as the participant.

Vendors such as ibl.ai, Coursebox and Edvisor sell tools that generate syllabi, course content and outcome-aligned course structures. These are their own marketing claims and were not independently verified.
A 2025 IEEE study found that no LLM produced a complete curriculum as good as human-built ones, but LLMs helped a lot when humans worked closely with them.

Kinesiology curriculum changes go through votes by department faculty and approval by the chair, college committees, the dean and the curriculum committee. This is institutional faculty governance, not a legal or licensing requirement.

Teacher license renewal requires the educator to complete professional learning personally. For example, Colorado requires 90 contact hours every 7 years and North Carolina requires 15 renewal units per 5-year cycle. An agent cannot earn the teacher's own competence or credit.

AI note-takers such as Read AI, Leexi and Zoom AI Companion can record, transcribe and summarize virtual professional-development sessions and conference talks. This helps the teacher, but the teacher still has to take part and absorb the learning.
Vendor case studies show AI summaries being used to track conference sessions and pick out key content. This speeds up the review and follow-up steps of attending, not the learning itself.

In a traditional hand pay, the slot machine locks and a casino employee pays the jackpot by hand, usually with a W-2G copy, then unlocks the machine. Software can fill in the form, but the payout and the signature are physical, face-to-face steps.

Louisiana rules require the slot attendant to get a valid ID, the patron's name, address and SSN, and the jackpot amount before paying out jackpots of $1,200 or more. This means the regulation puts responsibility for the step on a human attendant.

Hard Rock's Self-Pay Jackpot system keeps a stored electronic signature for W-2G forms and moves the jackpot to the machine's credit meter, so no attendant is needed for that payout. Software can replace parts of the process, but only through casino system redesign, not through an AI agent acting for the cashier.

Making a rubbed finish means wetting hardened concrete by hand and grinding it with a carborundum brick or similar abrasive until the color and texture are even, usually within 24 hours of removing the forms. The work is entirely manual and has to be done on site.

The worker moves coarse and then fine rubbing stones in circular strokes and has to control the pressure to avoid gouging the surface. A software-only agent with no robotic body cannot do any of this.

Industry commentary from an ACI-affiliated source treats rubbed finishes as a manual craft step whose feasibility depends on curing time and how strong the concrete mix is. The step is not linked to licensing or sign-off.

Under 49 CFR 396.11, the driver must complete a written or electronic inspection report that lists defects affecting safety. The next driver must review it and sign off that repairs were made. The finding and the signature have to come from a human driver.

Vendors sell voice-enabled and app-based electronic DVIRs that turn a driver's spoken or photo input into a structured defect report. This lets software handle the form-filling and paperwork side of the task.

Vendors say refuse-fleet telematics (J1939 fault codes, PTO hours) and yard-exit camera scanning can find some defects and create work orders automatically. These claims are unverified. Many defects on packers, hydraulics and lifts still need a person to inspect the truck and the equipment.

Game wardens describe public speaking as a large part of their outreach work. They prefer bringing physical visual aids, such as wildlife items, to slideshows, so the officer has to be there in person.

Conservation officers run in-person education and outreach, such as hunter education classes and school and community programs. The value of these programs depends on the uniformed officer being present and trusted.
AI presentation agents in 2026 can produce whole slide decks from a prompt and can even narrate them. That covers the preparation step, but an officer still has to give the talk or interview live.

O*NET's profile for Fish and Game Wardens (33-3031.00) describes fieldwork such as patrolling on foot, by vehicle, boat or aircraft, and protecting wildlife and habitat. The search summary did not show this maintenance task in O*NET's list, so the claim that the job is physical rests mainly on the task wording itself.

A New Mexico state job description says wardens spend much of their time writing reports and keeping records. Software can only touch side jobs like that (for example planning, ordering supplies or logging), not the hands-on building, repair, or weed and pest control.

Coin collection is hands-on work. Collectors pick up vault keys and sealed canisters, sign custody logs, physically open each meter and empty its coin can into a canister. Software cannot do any of this.

Software only handles the planning side. Vendor tools watch canister fill levels, send low/warning/critical alerts, plan just-in-time collection routes and reconcile cash totals by route, which shortens the work but does not remove the physical collection.
NYC DOT uses alerts from its Parkfolio software to set collection schedules, targeting meters at about 900 coins. Software sets the timing, and crews still collect the coins in person.

A vendor case study says a county animal services chatbot answers questions about lost and found pets, licensing, adoptions and welfare programs, and uses map data to give answers for the resident's own area. The results are self-reported.
Maricopa County's 24/7 AI assistant handles resident questions about county programs. Early data shows strong interest in pet services.
A shelter chatbot vendor claims, in its own marketing, that 80% of routine questions were resolved instantly. Harder cases still go to staff.
Georgia law defines barbering to include giving facial or scalp massages and treatments with oils or creams. This is a licensed, hands-on service.
Delaware law defines a barber as someone who, for pay, gives facial or scalp massages. That ties the service to a licensed human practitioner.

New Mexico barber rules cover facial and scalp massage and applying products to the scalp, face and neck. All of this is physical manipulation, which an AI agent that works only through software cannot do.

Vaccinating through drinking water or by spray is hands-on work. Someone has to prepare the water lines, make the birds thirsty, mix and dose the vaccine, finish giving it within 1.5 to 3 hours, and spray from about 50 cm away. An agent without a body can only help with the dose and dilution maths and with the timing plan.

Product labels set the reconstitution and dosing rules, for example 1,000 doses per litre per day of age. An agent could look these up and do the calculations, but a person still has to give the vaccine.

Automated vaccination for livestock exists only as robotics, such as RFID or vision-guided needle-free injectors, and is mostly at prototype or early-deployment stage. That falls outside a software-only agent.

Free online fence configurators already take animal species, area size, fence type and power supply and produce a material list you can export. An AI agent could also do this planning and quantity work, but that is a small part of the job.

Building a hutch means using a saw, drill, impact driver, staple gun, tin snips and hog-ring pliers to cut lumber, put up framing, fit wire mesh, hang doors and lay roofing. This is hands-on work that a software-only agent with no robot body cannot do.

University extension guidance on building farm fences covers post spacing, bracing and gates as on-site construction work. It does not mention any licence or sign-off needed for typical small animal pens.

Online livestock marketplaces like LivestockMarket.com already handle for-sale listings, inventory and sales management, and buyer messaging. An agent could post listings and answer inquiries through them.
Marketplaces such as Farmia let buyers search by location, category and price, and the platform also coordinates vet checks and transport. These logistics steps are digital and can be automated.

Under the USDA Animal Welfare Act, breeders who sell to research facilities need a USDA license (Class A or B). This applies to the business, not to a human signing each sale. Search results were mostly 2004 to 2017, so current rules were not confirmed. Final contract terms and relationship-based negotiation with institutional buyers still usually need human sign-off.

OSHA's forklift training rule (1910.178(l)) has three parts: formal instruction, practical training (demonstrations by the trainer and exercises by the trainee), and an evaluation of the operator's performance in the workplace. A person with hands-on knowledge, training and experience must do the training and evaluation, and the records name that trainer or evaluator.

Under the standard, operators must run the equipment while someone watches and evaluates them before they count as trained. The first evaluation should be done in a safe area under close supervision, so the hands-on demonstration needs a person on site.

VR forklift simulators from Raymond and Jungheinrich provide graded training levels and progress reports for instructors. These tools support digital parts of the job, such as tracking progress, choosing training tasks and preparing materials, but a human still demonstrates on real equipment.

Vendor material (not independently verified) describes predictive ETA tools that use GPS, hours-of-service and traffic data to flag loads that may be late. The vendor says these delay alerts go to dispatchers and customers automatically by email, SMS or EDI, so the routine delay-reporting part of the task can already be automated.

Telematics crash detection can send real-time crash alerts to fleets and pass data to emergency services. Still, in serious crashes a human often has to call and give details, and judging the scene, such as injuries or hazards, depends on the driver being there.

FMCSA rules allow commercial drivers to use hands-free phones and one-touch dialing. Push-to-talk phones that must be held are banned while driving, but CB and two-way radios are not covered. This supports voice-assistant relaying and does not create a requirement that a human perform the report.

Current AI tools such as Chalkie, Brisk and LessonCrafts generate slide decks, differentiated worksheets, flashcards and handouts from a topic, with export to Docs, Slides or PDF. So the digital part of preparing materials can be delegated end to end, though the instructor still checks it.

AI worksheet generators take a topic or pasted text and produce worksheets that can be printed or exported as PDFs. The agent cannot do the physical work of printing, gathering supplies, or arranging the room and equipment for hands-on classes like art, cooking, dance or music.

Several vendors offer lesson-material generators that export to PDF, Docs or Slides. No licence or sign-off is needed to prepare non-credit enrichment class materials, but setting up the classroom still needs someone there in person.

Claude in PowerPoint launched in February 2026 and reached Pro plans on February 20, 2026. It can build slides and make targeted edits to existing decks, so an agent can produce the presentation materials itself.
Claude Cowork can read a folder of files, plan a multi-step task and produce a finished .pptx. That lets an agent turn analysis files into a proposal deck end to end.

Vendors sell AI agents that write logistics proposals from templates and client data, though these are marketing claims rather than independent case studies. Delivering the proposal orally, answering questions and persuading stakeholders is still done by people.

Sanoma in Finland uses GPT-4o to write local forecasts for 26 regions from Finnish Meteorological Institute data, and a synthetic voice reads them on radio. Separately, a former US TV meteorologist runs AI avatars that produce 27 forecasts a day across nine markets.

The Weather Company's ReelSphere makes near real-time weather video clips for broadcast and social media, with an AI voice or a meteorologist's voice. Humans still write the scripts and correct errors.

The National Weather Service uses AI to translate its warnings and forecasts, which cut translation time from 1 hour to under 10 minutes. Forecasters still review the translations before release, and official warnings remain the responsibility of human forecasters.

A developer reports that Claude Code, running an agent interface for MODFLOW 6, built a groundwater model on its own: data import, grid, boundary conditions, wells, model runs and result checks. Human judgment is still needed for assumptions and for checking that results make sense. This is a vendor claim, the tool is in private beta, and the claim is not independently checked.
The AQUAH hydrology agent can run cold-start simulations and write documentation without manual steps, but its authors say calibration and validation are still needed before operational use.
In Washington State, a licensed geologist or hydrogeologist must stamp or seal, sign and date every final hydrogeologic report. Other states have similar rules.

Legal-aid chatbots such as Lone Star Legal Aid's Navi and Legal Aid of North Carolina's LIA already give people information, referrals and possible next steps around the clock. This shows an AI can handle the research-and-referral part of the task.

Illinois's WOPR Act (HB 1806, 2025) bars AI from directly interacting with therapy clients or making therapeutic decisions without review by a licensed clinician. Nevada has a similar restriction, so a licensed therapist has to review and deliver anything client-facing.

Under the same law, licensed professionals may still use AI for administrative and supplementary support with the client's written consent. Drafting a resource list for the therapist to review fits that, and the task needs no physical presence.

Museum guidance says objects chosen for an exhibit must be surveyed in person for condition and display vulnerability. The designer, conservator and curator then work together on display methods, so the hands-on examination is a step a human has to do.

Each object's condition assessment sets its display requirements, including light, humidity and case protection. If an agent is given the condition reports, photos and dimensions, it can turn them into a placement and mounting plan.

Using AI to plan museum layouts is still mostly at the research-prototype stage, such as generated floor plans for exhibition halls. A digital agent can still draft layout options and display plans from digitised object data.
Aftershoot automatically finds duplicates, blurry shots, closed eyes and other technical flaws. It then picks the best image from each group of similar shots, and the user can set how strict it is.

Narrative Select groups similar shots into scenes and ranks them by focus and whether eyes are open, but the photographer still makes the final rating and selection. FilterPixel can aim for a target number of final images.

Imagen's culling tool groups similar images so the photographer can choose the best one. In practice the human still reviews the AI's picks for artistic quality and fit with the client before delivery.

Food-service costing platforms such as Galley work out the cost per portion and the food-cost percentage of a recipe from its ingredient prices. When a supplier price changes, they recalculate the plate cost automatically and flag dishes that have fallen below the target margin.

Some restaurant systems read invoices to update ingredient prices and quantities automatically, and they save unit conversions such as cases to pounds. This covers the main data-entry and calculation steps with no physical presence needed.

Some recipe-costing apps suggest menu prices based on target food-cost percentages. The final price still depends on institutional policy, such as subsidies and fixed cafeteria or school price rules, so a manager typically reviews and approves it.

Hospital cleaning platforms such as MyCleaning, HealthClean and SmartView already handle the digital parts of the work: logging and prioritising cleaning requests, dispatching staff, verifying finished cleans and flagging hygiene risks. An agent could run these coordination steps.

In a 2026 trial, a computer-vision AI checked cleaning staff on-site against a nine-step procedure. This shows that checking how cleaning is done depends on physical, on-site observation, not on a software-only agent.

EVS supervisor duties include disinfecting contaminated areas, taking surface samples, setting cleaning methods and choosing disinfectants, and coaching staff on how infections spread. CMS assigns overall responsibility for the infection control program to the facility and its infection preventionists. It does not require the EVS supervisor personally to perform or sign this task.
Venue software such as Tripleseat Floorplans can draw room layouts and count tables, chairs and linens. That covers only the small planning part of the job; it does not physically set anything up.
Planur can count tables, chairs and linens automatically and share the layout with the crew, but people still have to carry out the setup by hand.
The main work is physical: moving and arranging tables, chairs, decorations, ladders and scaffolding. The reference agents have no body or robotics, so they can't do this part.

Polishing silver is hands-on work. You apply polish with a cloth using small circular motions, use a toothbrush or cotton swab for tight spots, then wipe and dry the piece by hand. A software agent with no robotics can't do any of this.

Housekeeping guides describe silver care as a physical, in-person process (prep, clean, polish, buff). The only part an AI could help with is advice on the method, such as which polish to use or whether to avoid dips, and that is a tiny share of the time spent.

Lawn care software can calculate application rates, spray mixes and treatment schedules, and can identify pests from photos. This covers only the planning sub-steps. Mixing chemicals and spraying or spreading them on site is physical work that a software-only agent cannot do.
Remote AI measurement of a property can supply the square footage used to work out fertilizer and herbicide quantities and application rates.
Anyone applying pesticides for pay on another person's property must hold a state commercial pesticide applicator license, earned by passing a core exam and a category exam such as lawn care.

Machines that plant automatically (Milrem's planter robot, the Continental/Land Life seeding robot) are robotics for reforestation fields. A software-only AI agent cannot run them, and they do not do landscape planting or mulching.
Planting robots that can dig holes, plant saplings and cover the soil are still mostly research prototypes. This shows the task is physical manipulation work.

Autonomous tree planting depends on robots with LiDAR and GPS working on site, which confirms the core work needs a physical body. A software agent could only help with small side steps like looking up planting guidance or scheduling.

Making a poured concrete border is hands-on work done on site: digging and compacting the trench, driving stakes, fastening hardboard or plywood forms, mixing and pouring concrete, troweling, cutting control joints, sealing and stripping the forms.
The manufacturer's method is also physical: compacted gravel base, forms with spacers, bagged crack-resistant mix poured and finished in place, with no software-run step an AI could do.

The only automation is mechanical curbing machines that push concrete through a mold. A person still has to steer them and control their speed and material flow, so there is no software or AI substitute. An agent could at most help with planning or working out how much concrete is needed.

AI recruiting agents available in 2026 handle sourcing, screening, outreach and scheduling end to end. Adoption is still partial: Bullhorn found 30% of firms using some agentic AI, and guides recommend that a human sign off on final hiring decisions.

NYC Local Law 144 requires annual independent bias audits and candidate notices for automated employment decision tools. The EU AI Act classes employment AI as high-risk, with risk-management, transparency and documentation duties, which keeps a human accountable for hiring and evaluation decisions.

Sources warn that automated screening with no human review before the offer stage is where bias and compliance risk concentrate. They recommend human sign-off and audit logs, so final hiring and evaluation judgments stay with the supervisor.

Dedicated scanning hardware now does much of the data capture. LoadMon 3D truck scanners measure load volume, diameter and skew in under two minutes, and Woodtech LogMeter scales logs from photos of the log ends. Both need sensors at the mill or yard, not just a software agent.

Scalers type tally data into handheld computers or write it on tickets while standing at the logs, then send it to the main office. The data comes from in-person measurement, so recording it is tied to being on site.
In Idaho it is illegal to scale logs for commercial use unless you hold a licence or are an apprentice supervised by a licensed scaler, so a human scaler is accountable for the recorded scale.

Log-load measurement is being automated with fixed hardware such as Woodtech LogMeter's camera portals and LoadMon's 3D truck scanners at mill intake. These are sensors installed on site, not software agents, and they do not replace a person driving to sawmills, wharfs or skids to inspect logs.
Idaho law requires anyone scaling logs commercially to be licensed by the Board of Scaling Practices, and getting the licence means passing written and practical exams.
Idaho's Board of Scaling Practices requires a practical exam for the licence and a re-examination every two years at renewal.

Elevat's AI Technician Assistant (Feb 2026) turns machine telemetry, fault codes, service manuals and repair history into prioritized repair steps. It advises the technician but does not do the repair itself.
Cummins Connected Diagnostics lets off-highway equipment send engine fault alerts wirelessly for remote diagnosis. That is software help with diagnosis only, not the physical maintenance work.
A practitioner guide notes that AI cannot disassemble, repair or reassemble heavy mechanical components. That hands-on work makes up most of this task.

Line-side replenishment depends on a warehouse system that reads consumption signals from the line and issues replenishment tasks. The software handles the planning and triggering, while people or vehicles carry the materials.

In electronics assembly, SMD reel replenishment software works out real-time demand from consumption and sends requests to the reel warehouse. That covers the digital planning sub-step, but the reels still have to be delivered to the line physically.
Moving materials to the line is physical work. It is done by operators, or by robots, tuggers and AMRs triggered by the warehouse system. A software-only agent with no robotics cannot do it.

Plating-line production logs record bath chemistry, temperature, current density, voltage, rinse checks and corrective actions, with one entry and a sign-off per shift. The source readings come from the shop floor, by hand or from instruments.

Plating ERP and maintenance tools can track amp-hours, titration logs and lot traceability, and link rectifier logs to timestamped records. But reviews say automated shop-floor data capture is weak in some tools, and many still rely on manual entry.

EPA Subpart N requires chromium electroplating facilities to keep monitoring, inspection and maintenance records for 5 years, with dates and times. The rule requires the records to exist but does not say a licensed person must prepare them.

AI tools such as Air Space Intelligence's Flyways at Alaska Airlines already study weather, winds, turbulence, airspace and traffic, and suggest optimised routes and fuel changes to dispatchers and pilots. The suggestions are advisory. Dispatchers take them only about 30% of the time, and the final decision stays with people.

Jeppesen Dispatch automates checking routes and recalculating flight plans that balance cost, time and fuel. This means the computing part of a change to route, fuel or load can be done by software from start to finish.

Under 14 CFR 91.3 the pilot in command is directly responsible for the flight and is its final authority. Under 121.533 the PIC and a licensed dispatcher share responsibility for preflight planning and the dispatch release, and in flight the PIC is responsible for safety. So a human has to make and own the decision to order the change.

Installing and repairing rails and ties is heavy manual work. Workers remove and replace crossties, lift and carry track material of 50 to 70 lb, shovel ballast, and use hand tools and maintenance-of-way machines outdoors in all weather. A software-only agent cannot do any of this.
Tie gangs work with on-site machinery such as tampers, spike inserters and pullers, tie cranes, and tie extractors and inserters. People must be physically present to run these machines.

Under FRA Roadway Worker Protection rules (49 CFR 214 Subpart C), roadway workers need annual training, and roadway maintenance machine operators must prove they can run the machines. This means trained humans have to be on the track.

Card payment at fuel dispensers is already automated by EMV/PCI-certified outdoor payment terminals and card readers built into the pump. These are fixed devices on the forecourt that the customer uses directly. They are not AI agents.

At some marinas, fuel is sold through apps or tag-on-account systems with no staff on site. This makes the payment digital. It replaces the attendant with self-service rather than with an agent that does the attendant's work.

On staffed fuel docks, attendants still run a mobile POS app to tender card sales and put purchases on account. An agent could process the digital parts (account charges, receipts), but taking cash and making change needs a person on site.
